props.title: The Racket

sections.content: The Racket stands as a pivotal pre-Code crime film that helped establish the template for police corruption narratives. Director Lewis Milestone crafted a gritty portrayal of Chicago-style organized crime that directly influenced later classics like The Public Enemy (1931) and Little Caesar (1931). The film's unflinching look at police corruption and political machinery was so controversial that certain cities initially banned it, fearing it would damage public trust in law enforcement.

sections.content: The film's technical innovations were remarkable for 1928. Milestone's dynamic camera movements and atmospheric lighting techniques influenced film noir's visual style a decade later. The night scenes in particular, with their stark shadows and rain-slicked streets, prefigure the work of later noir masters like John Huston in The Asphalt Jungle (1950) and Jules Dassin in The Naked City (1948).

Howard Hughes' involvement as producer helped ensure the film's uncompromising approach to corruption. Unlike many contemporary crime films that were forced to show crime doesn't pay, The Racket presents a more nuanced view of systemic corruption that would become impossible under strict enforcement of the Production Code after 1934. This makes it a crucial bridge between the silent era's relatively unfettered crime dramas and the more restrictive gangster films of the 1930s. SUBHEAD: Impact on Crime Cinema

The film's influence extends beyond its immediate era. Its portrayal of the lone honest cop fighting a corrupt system became a template for countless films, from Serpico (1973) to L.A. Confidential (1997). The character dynamics between Thomas Meighan's incorruptible Captain McQuigg and Louis Wolheim's brutal gangster Nick Scarsi established the cop-criminal antagonist relationship that would become a genre staple.
